```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(zulake)
```

A Delta Lake table is a folder of Parquet files plus a log that says which
files make up each version. Reading the files without the log returns
deleted and superseded rows. zulake reads the log itself: on this page we
open a table, look inside its log, and then read it with a filter. Reading
a table on Azure is the last section; everything before it runs on a table
that ships with the package.

## Open a table

The example table holds a few orders, partitioned by `region`, written in
five commits on five days. `lake_open()` builds a **snapshot** of one
version, the latest unless you ask for another.

```{r}
path <- system.file("extdata", "orders", package = "zulake")
tbl <- lake_open(path)
tbl
```

A snapshot never changes. `lake_versions()` lists the versions the log
still holds, with the time each was committed, and `lake_load()` gives you
a snapshot of another one, by number or by time.

```{r}
lake_versions(tbl)
old <- lake_load(tbl, timestamp = as.POSIXct("2025-01-08 12:00", tz = "UTC"))
lake_version(old)
```

## The log as data frames

Inspection is what zulake is for. Each function answers one question from
the log alone, as a base data frame, with nested values in list columns.
The history says what each commit did:

```{r}
lake_history(tbl)[c("version", "timestamp", "operation")]
lake_schema(tbl)[c("name", "type", "partition")]
```

`lake_files()` lists the files of the snapshot with their partition values
and statistics; `lake_count()` adds up the row counts the statistics
record, without reading a file.

```{r}
files <- lake_files(tbl)
files[c("path", "size_bytes", "num_records")]
lake_count(tbl)
```

Version 3 deleted one order. `lake_actions()` shows that commit as the log
holds it, and `lake_changes()` the files it took away and added: the file
that held the order is replaced by one with its other rows.

```{r}
lake_actions(tbl, version = 3)[c("line", "type")]
lake_changes(tbl, from = 2, to = 3)[c("change", "path")]
```

The last commit also recorded the version of the application that wrote
it, which a loader uses to avoid writing the same batch twice:

```{r}
lake_transactions(tbl)
```

Counts, sizes and statistics are 64-bit in the log. They come back as
doubles, exact up to 2^53 - 1, and an error beyond; ask for
`int64 = "integer64"` to get `bit64` integers instead.

## Filters prune files, then rows

A **filter** is an R expression over column names. Partition values and
statistics rule out files that cannot match before anything is read: of
the twelve files, only two can hold an order from the EU over 1000.

```{r}
lake_files(tbl, filter = region == "EU" & amount > 1000)$path
```

`lake_read()` reads the files that remain and then filters their rows, so
the result never depends on the statistics. Local values are looked up
where you call, and dates compare as dates.

```{r}
since <- as.Date("2025-01-08")
lake_read(tbl, columns = c("order_id", "customer", "amount"),
          filter = order_date >= since & amount > 300)
```

Besides comparisons, a filter may use row-wise functions such as
`nchar()`, `round()` or arithmetic, which filter rows but never rule out
files. A call that looks at other rows is an error, because its answer
would depend on how the table is split into files:

```{r, error = TRUE}
lake_read(tbl, filter = amount > mean(amount))
```

`lake_walk()` reads one file at a time and hands each piece to a function,
for a table larger than memory:

```{r}
total <- 0
lake_walk(tbl, function(piece) total <<- total + sum(piece$amount),
          filter = region == "US")
total
```

## Deletion vectors and other features

Tables written by Databricks often delete rows by marking them in a
**deletion vector** rather than rewriting the file as the delete above
did. zulake never returns a marked row. `lake_deletion_vectors()` shows
each file's vector and the rows it deletes; this table has none. Reading
those rows needs the zuroar package, while the descriptors and
`lake_count()` come from the log alone.

```{r}
lake_deletion_vectors(tbl, rows = FALSE)
```

A table that needs a reader feature zulake does not support is refused,
with an error that names the feature, before any data is read, because
ignoring the feature would return wrong rows. `lake_protocol()` shows the
features a table uses, each marked supported; this one uses in-commit
timestamps, which only writers must know about.

```{r}
lake_protocol(tbl)
```

## Tables on Azure

The same functions read a table on Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 or Blob
Storage. You supply a function that returns a Microsoft Entra ID token for
Azure Storage; zulake calls it before its first request and again if Azure
says the token has expired, and never stores, prints or saves the token.
Here the token comes from the Azure CLI (not run on this page):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
token <- function() {
  system2("az", c(
    "account", "get-access-token", "--resource", "https://storage.azure.com",
    "--query", "accessToken", "--output", "tsv"
  ), stdout = TRUE)
}
tbl <- lake_open("abfss://lake@account.dfs.core.windows.net/sales/orders",
                 credentials = token)
lake_files(tbl, filter = region == "EU")
```

The same table is also
`https://account.dfs.core.windows.net/lake/sales/orders` or
`https://account.blob.core.windows.net/lake/sales/orders`.

  compare.
- `?lake_files` describes each column of the file list and the statistics.
- `?lake_open` covers versions, timestamps, Azure URIs and credentials.
- The [reference](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zulake/reference/index.html)
  lists every function.
